accepted.title: One month ago, Andrej Karpathy (founding member at OpenAI) posted something that stormed Twitter about LLM Knowledge Bases, and it perfectly illustrates what we are building.
accepted.text:
One month ago, Andrej Karpathy (founding member at OpenAI) posted something that stormed Twitter about LLM Knowledge Bases, and it perfectly illustrates what we are building. 

The idea is simple: you dump raw data sources, papers, tables, repos, and let an LLM turn all of it into a structured wiki. Summaries, backlinks, concept articles, all auto-generated and maintained by the model.

Once the knowledge base is built, you can ask real questions and the LLM will come back with actual answers.

People often talk about the great output they can get, but few talk about everything that had to happen before it.

The data had to be clean, structured, consistent. Without it, even the smartest system just hallucinates with confidence.

Karpathy does it himself with scripts and Obsidian. Most companies don't have an OpenAI cofounder to take care of their data. 

Most companies have real-world data: messy, scattered, inconsistent. 

That's exactly the problem we're building on: an agent that does the work a great data scientist would do, so you can orchestrate AI systems around a solid backbone to reason on. 

Netter is here to help any company get ready for the biggest technological shift of our era.

More details coming soon! 

Link of the tweet: https://lnkd.in/evh-Kepq

accepted.title: People overuse LLMs.
accepted.text:
People overuse LLMs.

One of the most common misconceptions in AI today is to assume that every intelligent system should be an LLM.

LLMs are extraordinary, but they are language models i.e optimized to understand and generate sequences of tokens.

The fact that they can answer questions, write code or analyze documents so well sometimes makes us forget that they were not designed to solve every problem.

If you want to forecast demand, predict equipment failures, optimize a production schedule, or detect anomalies in financial transactions, many ML models (Gradient Boosting, Time-series forecasting models etc.) will often outperform an LLM.

In many cases, a deterministic algorithm will be more reliable, easier to validate, and orders of magnitude cheaper to run.

What makes the current wave of AI so exciting is not that LLMs replace everything else. It is that they provide a universal interface to all these capabilities. They can understand a user's intent, gather context, orchestrate workflows and decide when to invoke forecasting models, optimization engines, or other business rules.

Like a conductor who knows when to call upon the sustained reliability of the strings, the surgical precision of the oboe, the raw power of the tuba or the split-second accuracy of the percussion. The LLM knows which intelligence to summon, and when.

In that sense, LLMs are often more of a means than an end.

The future of enterprise AI will belong to systems capable of combining multiple forms of machine intelligence and applying the most relevant one to solve a specific problem.

That's the philosophy behind Netter's product: making organizations AI-ready so agents can deploy the right intelligence for each task, whether it's an LLM, a forecasting model, a deterministic algorithm or even a simple SQL query.

accepted.title: We're hiring another Customer Success Manager at Dayjob to support our growing customer base.
accepted.text:
We're hiring another Customer Success Manager at Dayjob to support our growing customer base.

We build AI agents for waste trucks, one of the largest, least-digitised sectors of the economy. 

This year we got backed by Y Combinator, are live with 13 paying customers, and are growing fast.

Our customers run real fleets, with real operational complexity. A 5% improvement in routing efficiency is worth hundreds of thousands of pounds a year to them. We take that seriously. 

We want every customer to feel the impact of what we're building, and this role is central to making that happen.

This is a field-first role: three days a week at customer depots across the UK, the rest at our Camden office. You'll own a portfolio of accounts end-to-end, drive measurable efficiency gains, and help build the CS function from the ground up.

The kind of person who will love this:

- Gets energy from being on-site and around straight-talking people 
- Wants to build something from scratch
- Takes full ownership and doesn't wait to be told

£50k to £90k depending on level of experience, plus equity.

Full details in the spec in comments. If someone in your network would be a great fit, tag them or send it their way.

accepted.title: The June Secured Finance Network webinar on fraud risk opened with a line worth sitting with.
accepted.text:
The June Secured Finance Network webinar on fraud risk opened with a line worth sitting with.

"As ERPs evolve, payments go fully digital, and bad actors deploy generative AI, traditional monitoring tools are no longer enough."

That's not a warning about the future. It's a description of right now.

Here's what that means in practice for a factoring desk running standard document review:

The fraud that used to take weeks to engineer now takes hours. A borrower who wants to manufacture a receivable can use generative AI to produce an invoice in correct formatting, plausible buyer name, consistent with the borrower's historical style, all in minutes. The document passes visual inspection because it was designed to.

Your analyst reviews it. Approves it. You fund.

The fraud detection gap isn't analyst skill. It's detection architecture. Manual review was built for a world where fraud required significant effort to produce. That world ended.

The checks that now matter can't be run by eye:

Metadata validation: does the file's creation date match the stated invoice date?
Cross-portfolio duplicate detection: was this same receivable submitted to another lender this week?
Buyer registry verification: does this entity actually exist and operate at this scale?
Relationship plausibility: does the transaction size match the buyer-seller history?

None of these take more than seconds when automated. All of them take longer than a typical review cycle when done manually, which means they don't get done.

The cost of a funded fraudulent invoice isn't a write-down. It's a realized loss. And when the LP asks for the audit trail, the question won't be whether fraud occurred. It'll be whether the system was designed to catch it.

Most operations today are running detection designed for the last generation of fraud.

The current generation of fraud was designed with that in mind.
Let’s change this together. Hit us up at hi@zolvo.com

The June issue of The Secured Lender ran a piece titled "Protecting Collateral Liquidity Through Cyber Operational Resilience." One paragraph has been circulating in ABL circles since.

"In a cyber incident, collateral may remain 'there' but visibility to the lender's collateral and its quality disappears. If a borrower can't ship, can't invoice, or can't produce a trustworthy borrowing base for even a few days, collateral proceeds and AR/inventory mix will change significantly."

That's the hidden operational risk almost no servicing team models for.

Here's the structure of the problem:

ABL is built on the premise that collateral converts to cash if the borrower defaults. But that conversion depends on a live, accurate picture of what the collateral actually is at any given moment. AR aging. Invoice mix. Inventory levels. Dilution rates.

When that picture goes dark, whether because of a cyber incident, a system failure, or simply a manual process that can't update fast enough, the lender is flying without instruments.

The borrowing base certificate becomes stale the moment it's submitted. By the time the next one arrives, the collateral composition has already shifted. A lender relying on periodic manual reporting is always operating on a lag.

The operational consequence isn't theoretical. It shows up in advance rate calculations that don't reflect current eligibility. In concentration limits that breach silently. In covenant monitoring that catches problems after they've compounded.

The lenders who aren't exposed to this risk aren't running better field exams. They're running continuous monitoring: real-time data feeds from bank accounts and receivables systems, automatic borrowing base recalculation, covenant alerts that fire before breach rather than after.

The infrastructure gap between a periodic manual process and a continuous one is where most collateral risk lives in 2026. Not in credit quality, in visibility latency. 

Let Zolvo handle this, improve your visibility now. Hit us up at hi@zolvo.com

accepted.title: Six months ago, a mid-market lender got a routine LP data request.
accepted.text:
Six months ago, a mid-market lender got a routine LP data request.

"Can you pull the confirmation records for the supply chain facilities from Q4?"

Standard ask. Thirty-minute job, they assumed.

Four business days later, they were still reconstructing.

The confirmation records existed... 
somewhere, but, where?)

Spread across three email inboxes, two shared drives, a folder labeled "2025 Verification Misc," and a spreadsheet someone had built to track things manually before realizing it was too slow to maintain. The analyst who had run most of those confirmations was on parental leave.

They found what they needed. Eventually. But the LP had moved on and was now asking a different question: not about Q4, but about their verification process in general.

ABF Journal covered a version of this story in a different context last week, noting that "documentation, audit rights and confirmation protocols are all being rebuilt" across the asset class following verification gaps that surfaced in supply chain financing last year. The exposure wasn't the fraud itself. It was the absence of a clean, timestamped record of what the lender had checked and when.

What LP due diligence looks like now is different from what it looked like two years ago. The question has shifted from "do you have the data?" to "can you show me the process that produced it?"

A spreadsheet answer to that question used to be acceptable.

It isn't anymore.

The operations that can answer that question in minutes rather than days aren't running harder. They're running with a different system: one where the verification record is created automatically at the moment of confirmation, not reconstructed four days later when someone asks.

Leave audit trails to Zolvo, hit us up at hi@zolvo.com

accepted.title: "Private Credit in 2026: Discipline, Dispersion and Defaults" by Arcesium makes a point operators already suspect: default outcomes get decided long before the default shows up on
accepted.text:
"Private Credit in 2026: Discipline, Dispersion and Defaults" by Arcesium  makes a point operators already suspect: default outcomes get decided long before the default shows up on paper, in how early the operational team notices stress and how fast that signal reaches the right person.

Most servicing teams already have that signal. It just doesn't travel.

A collections analyst notices a borrower asking for three payment extensions in six weeks. Notes it in the CRM. Moves to the next call.

A reconciliation analyst, working a different queue entirely, notices the same borrower's payments have started arriving four to six days late, every month, for the last quarter.

Neither analyst sees the other's notes. Neither one is wrong. The information just lives in two systems that don't talk, updated by two people who don't compare notes unless something has already gone wrong enough to force a meeting.

By the time both signals reach a risk officer together, the borrower isn't early-stage stressed anymore. They're 60 days out, and the workout conversation starts from a weaker position than it needed to.

The whitepaper's framing: technology integration matters less as a productivity story and more as a signal-routing story. The extension requests and the late payments were never separate data points. They were the same borrower, in the same quarter, telling the same story twice, to two people who never compared notes.

Fixing this isn't hiring a risk analyst to read every note. It's making the collections log and the reconciliation ledger reference the same borrower record, so the pattern surfaces on its own instead of waiting for a human to notice it twice.

How are you preventing or solving this gap?🧐

accepted.title: We never thought we'd compare Zolvo to a referee.
accepted.text:
We never thought we'd compare Zolvo to a referee. But here we are.

Think about VAR for a second.

The referee runs the whole match. Makes the call. Keeps things moving.
VAR only gets checked when something looks wrong.

That's exactly how Zolvo works for accounting teams.

Every reconciliation. Every debtor pool update. Every NOA. Every transaction running quietly in the background.

Zolvo makes the call. In real time. No human needed to babysit it.

Your accounting team doesn't touch it (they don't have to).

They only step in when something's actually exceptional. A mismatch. A flag. Something that needs a real human decision.

That's it. That's the whole job now.

Not reviewing 100% of transactions like it's still 2015.
Just reviewing the 2% that actually matter.

We built this because we watched teams manually checking EVERY play when they should've been trusting the system and only stepping in for the controversial calls.

The best referees are invisible. You only notice them when something's wrong.

That's the product we're building.

accepted.title: What should we talk about when focusing on niche lending: construction, oilfield services, staffing?
accepted.text:
What should we talk about when focusing on niche lending: construction, oilfield services, staffing?

SFNet's panel spent an hour on one idea: the red flags in these industries don't look like red flags anywhere else.

A regional factor decided to test that against their own book. They ran an audit on 90 days of construction invoices.

What they found:

One: pay-if-paid clauses buried in subcontracts that made half their "eligible" receivables conditional on a payment that hadn't happened yet.

Two: three invoices from the same GC, same project, submitted by two different subcontractors they were funding. Same job, same money, funded twice.

Three: a staffing sub-vertical where the invoice amount tracked headcount that didn't match any payroll filing on record.

None of these tripped a standard fraud check. Standard checks look for forged documents and inflated amounts. These were real documents, real numbers, wrong assumptions.

The panel's point: construction, oilfield, and staffing all carry industry-specific structures, retainage, joint checks, pay-if-paid, per diem staffing math, that a generic verification process was never built to catch.

The factor's fix wasn't more review time. It was industry-specific rules layered onto the standard checks: flag pay-if-paid language automatically, cross-reference GC and project across submissions, tie staffing invoices to headcount data.

Same team. Same volume. Different questions being asked of every invoice.

accepted.title: ABF Journal's read on this week: higher-for-longer cost of capital, collateral-anchored underwriting, borrowing-base discipline.
accepted.text:
ABF Journal's read on this week: higher-for-longer cost of capital, collateral-anchored underwriting, borrowing-base discipline. That's the environment every commercial lender is underwriting into right now.

Here's the number that environment doesn't show up in, but should: what your current manual servicing process is costing you per month, separate from your cost of capital.

Take a mid-size factoring shop running $80M in receivables. Three reconciliation analysts at $75K a year. If 40% of their time goes to fixing errors and rework instead of new volume, that's roughly $90,000 a year spent correcting a process instead of running it.

Add invoice fraud that slips past manual review because a 60-invoice batch doesn't get six layers of checking, it gets two. Add a borrowing base certificate that's a week behind the actual reconciled ledger by the time an LP or auditor asks for it.

None of that shows up as a line item. It shows up as a slower close, a covenant question nobody can answer cleanly, and a fraud loss that gets discovered eighteen months later in a portfolio review.

In a higher-for-longer environment, capital is already more expensive. Layering an unmeasured servicing cost on top of that is a choice, even when it doesn't feel like one.

The question worth asking this quarter: if reconciliation, invoice verification, and borrowing-base reporting ran on current data instead of last week's export, what would that actually be worth against the cost of capital already being paid?

accepted.text:
If you’ve ever had an entire workflow break because a borrower updated their accounting software and renamed a spreadsheet column from Inv_Date to Billing_Date, you already know how brittle traditional automation is.

Everyone keeps saying "just use AI." or "give it to claude"

But the reality is that an AI error isn't just an awkward typo in a marketing email. It’s an undetected cross-aging dilution, a corrupted ineligible calculation, or an over-advance that vaporizes your collateral cushion.

The truth? AI is an incredible precision tool, but dropping it into a 30-year-old core system without customized data engineering, ontop of processes that are discretional to each employee, not knowing what to ask or what to expect is an existential risk to your capital and your reputation.

We do believe that AI can make your operations run smoother, but we know it's not just waving the magic wand.

accepted.title: From the cover of Nature to the agents of Netter (YC P26).
accepted.text:
From the cover of Nature to the agents of Netter (YC P26).

During my internship at AMOLF (Amsterdam), I wrote an algorithm that made the cover of Nature.

The lab was drowning in data: a single fungus generated ~700 GB of microscope images in two months, and a full experiment meant tens of terabytes a month. They could only study a handful of these organisms, by hand.

I built an algorithm to fix that: turn thousands of images into one compact map of the network, with the exact moment each branch grew baked in. Around 1000x smaller, and for the first time the team could analyze the entire dataset.

The network (every branch colored by its age) got featured on the cover of Nature.

That experience inspired me to build Netter (YC P26).

No matter how smart the LLM, what limits us is getting messy information into a shape intelligence can actually use.

Most companies have the exact same problem, at scale. Years of valuable data, scattered across tools that don’t talk to each other, and teams analyzing a sliver of it by hand.

Our mission is to democratize data science excellence: normalize and organize data so AI agents can reason across it and deploy the right intelligence for each situation.

We are now applying the same approach to entire companies (instead of fungi), with results already in production.

And we’re just getting started.
